Where it began

Mohammed Shami grew up in Sahaspur, a village in the Amroha district of Uttar Pradesh, one of five in a family where cricket came naturally. His father had bowled fast as a young man, and all three of his brothers played; one of them, Mohammed Kaif, went on to play for Bengal. At 15 Shami was taken to a coach, Badruddin Siddique, in nearby Moradabad, and after matches he would ask for the used balls so he could learn to make them reverse.

When a place in the state youth side did not come, his coach sent him to Kolkata in 2005. There a club official, Debabrata Das, took him into his own home and into his club, and Shami bowled his way into the Bengal under-22 side. A spell in the Eden Gardens nets against Sourav Ganguly did the rest: Ganguly put in a word, and Shami was picked for Bengal's Ranji Trophy squad in 2010–11.

The player

He made his Test debut at Eden Gardens, his adopted home ground, against the West Indies in November 2013, and took nine wickets for 118, the best by an Indian fast bowler on debut. From 2013 to 2023 he played 64 Tests and took 229 wickets at 27.71, with six five-wicket hauls and a best of 6 for 56. In South Africa in 2021–22 he became the fifth Indian pace bowler to 200 Test wickets, and got there in fewer balls than any of them.

He was just as dangerous in one-day cricket. At the 2023 World Cup he took 24 wickets, more than anyone, including 7 for 57 in the semi-final, and he was part of the side that won the Champions Trophy in 2025.

What made him special

His great gift was seam and swing, the ball moving both ways and often late, with reverse swing as his speciality. He liked to hit the stumps, and many of his wickets were bowled. The former India coach Ravi Shastri called him the Sultan of Bengal.

With the bat he was less fearsome, averaging a little over 12. Yet he twice made Test fifties, including a stand of 111 for the last wicket with Bhuvneshwar Kumar at Trent Bridge in 2014, and an unbeaten 56 in 2021 that helped India to a famous win over England.

Away from the middle

He received the Arjuna Award in January 2024. During the lockdown of 2020 he trained with his brother back home in Sahaspur, and the family made sure their neighbours in the village had food. In November 2023 he stopped on a hill road near Nainital to rescue a man caught in a road accident.

And finally

He spent his youth collecting other people's old cricket balls. It was time well spent: very few bowlers have made a worn ball misbehave quite so well.
